title: The Immune System at a Glance: Hypersensitivity Types and Their Lab Footprints
summary: Pair CD4 and CD8 with HLA class II and I, sort hypersensitivity into antibody-mediated types I–III and cell-mediated type IV (with the newer EAACI subtypes), and match each type to a laboratory test.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 44 Hits 1 and 3 and Traps 1–2 (first lesson for Ch. 44). Checked against Szegedi 2025 (EAACI addendum), Zarei 2026, Schroeder & Cavacini 2010, Althaf 2017, Al-Shaikhly 2020, Ansotegui 2020, Beck 2019 and Pai 2014. Nuance: the reviewer uses the classic four types; the 2023 EAACI nomenclature splits type IV into IVa–c and adds types V–VII. Not taught as fact: CD4:CD8 2:1 and subset percentages, Th1/Th2 and Treg/FOXP3 details, NK markers, checkpoint and CAR-T drugs, CD21/EBV, eculizumab/rituximab, multiplex vs ELISA dsDNA, cytokine measurement; TREC, CH50, syphilis algorithm and SPEP are taught in other lessons.

objectives: Pair CD4 and CD8 with the HLA classes they recognize.
Distinguish antibody-mediated types I–III from cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity.
Match each hypersensitivity type to a laboratory test that reflects its mechanism.

scenes.title: Four reactions, four lab answers
scenes.altText: Four invented requisitions on one bench: (1) tryptase after sudden hypotension and hives during surgery; (2) a CDC crossmatch that killed donor lymphocytes; (3) low C3 in a patient with active lupus nephritis; (4) an interferon-γ release assay for TB exposure. Question token: “Which hypersensitivity mechanism does each test look at?”

cues.text: Four requests arrive: tryptase after a reaction during surgery, and a crossmatch that killed donor lymphocytes.
Low C3 in a patient with active lupus nephritis, and an interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis.
Which immune mechanism is each test looking at?

props.label: Which mechanism does each test see?

scenes.title: Who presents to whom, and the classic four types
scenes.altText: Recognition card (Zarei 2026): CD8⁺ T cells recognize peptides on HLA class I; CD4⁺ helper T cells recognize antigens on HLA class II, and help B cells make antibody. Classification card (Szegedi 2025, addendum to the 2023 EAACI nomenclature): Type I — antibody-mediated IMMEDIATE reaction; Type II — antibody-mediated CYTOTOXIC reaction; Type III — antibody-mediated IMMUNE-COMPLEX reaction; Type IV — CELL-mediated reactions, now split into IVa (T1), IVb (T2) and IVc (T3). EAACI adds tissue-driven types V (epithelial) and VI (metabolic) and VII (direct response to chemicals).

cues.text: First, the pairing that never changes: CD8 cells read HLA class I; CD4 helper cells read class II and help B cells make antibody.
Hypersensitivity is an immune response that causes harm. Types one to three are driven by antibody: an immediate reaction, a cytotoxic reaction against cells, and an immune-complex reaction.
Type four is driven by T cells. The current European nomenclature splits it into three subtypes, a, b and c.
That nomenclature also adds tissue-driven and chemical types five to seven, but the classic four remain the core of most exams.

props.label: CD8 ↔ class I · CD4 ↔ class II

scenes.title: What harms the tissue in each type
scenes.altText: Mechanism cards (schematic). Type I: IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils is cross-linked by allergen → mediator release (Schroeder & Cavacini 2010). Type II: antibody binds antigen ON A CELL SURFACE and destroys that cell — e.g. donor-specific antibody plus complement kills donor lymphocytes in a CDC crossmatch (Althaf 2017). Type III: soluble antigen–antibody complexes deposit in tissues and consume complement — e.g. low C3 in SLE (Al-Shaikhly 2020). Type IV: sensitized T cells respond on re-exposure — e.g. memory T cells release interferon-γ to TB antigens (Pai 2014).

cues.text: Type one: allergen cross-links IgE already sitting on mast cells and basophils, and they release their mediators.
Type two: antibody binds an antigen that is part of a cell surface and destroys that cell, for example with complement.
Type three: antibody and soluble antigen form complexes that lodge in tissues and use up complement, as in active lupus.
Type four: no antibody needed. Sensitized T cells respond when they meet the antigen again, releasing cytokines such as interferon-gamma.

scenes.title: Matching tests to mechanisms
scenes.altText: Mapping card. Type I → serum specific IgE (sensitization) and mast-cell tryptase after a reaction: peak ~1–2 h, baseline ≥ 24 h, rise > 1.2 × baseline + 2 μg/L (Ansotegui 2020; Beck 2019). Type II → assays of antibody against cells: a CDC crossmatch shows recipient antibody plus complement killing donor lymphocytes (Althaf 2017). Type III → complement consumption: C3 can fall, sometimes to very low or undetectable levels, in SLE (Al-Shaikhly 2020). Type IV → T-cell response: IGRAs measure IFN-γ released by sensitized T cells (Pai 2014). Hook answers: (1) type I; (2) type II; (3) type III; (4) type IV.

cues.text: Each type has its laboratory footprint. For type one, measure specific IgE for sensitization, and after a reaction, tryptase at one to two hours with a baseline later.
For type two, look for antibody attacking cells, such as a crossmatch where recipient antibody and complement kill donor lymphocytes.
For type three, look for complement consumption: C3 can be very low in active lupus.
For type four, measure the T-cell response itself, as an interferon-gamma release assay does. So the four requests map to types one, two, three and four.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Type II is immune-complex disease” (✓ type II = antibody against a CELL; type III = soluble immune complexes depositing in tissue); “CD4 binds class I” (✓ CD8 ↔ class I, CD4 ↔ class II — “8 × 1 = 8, 4 × 2 = 8”); “Type IV reactions need antibody” (✓ type IV is cell-mediated — sensitized T cells, no antibody required).

cues.text: Trap one: type two is immune-complex disease. No: type two is antibody against a cell. Soluble immune complexes depositing in tissue are type three.
Trap two: CD4 binds class I. No: CD8 with class I, CD4 with class II. Eight times one is eight, four times two is eight.
Trap three: type four needs antibody. No: it is cell-mediated, driven by sensitized T cells.

props.title: ✗ “Type II = immune complexes.”
lines: ✓ II = antibody vs cell · III = complexes

scenes.title: ACID
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “A-C-I-D: Anaphylactic/immediate (I), Cytotoxic (II), Immune complex (III), Delayed/T-cell (IV).” Tokens: A = I · C = II · I = III · D = IV. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ACID. Anaphylactic or immediate is type one, cytotoxic is type two, immune complex is type three, and delayed, T-cell-mediated, is type four.

Where it breaks: real diseases often mix types; the current European nomenclature splits type four into three subtypes and adds types five to seven; and type four itself has three subtypes driven by different T-cell programmes.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Type IV has subtypes a, b, c

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “I immediate (IgE, mast cells) · II cytotoxic (antibody vs cell) · III immune complex (complement use) · IV T-cell · CD8↔I, CD4↔II”, “Lab: sIgE/tryptase · CDC crossmatch · low C3 · IGRA”.

cues.text: Types one to three of hypersensitivity are antibody-mediated, immediate, cytotoxic and immune-complex, while type four is T-cell-mediated, and each leaves a laboratory footprint: IgE and tryptase, cell-killing antibody, complement consumption, or T-cell cytokine release.

props.label: I IgE · II antibody vs cell · III complexes · IV T cells · CD8↔I, CD4↔II
Lab: sIgE/tryptase · CDC crossmatch · low C3 · IGRA

explanation.what: Plain language: harmful immune reactions come in a few basic kinds — allergy-type reactions within minutes, antibodies attacking cells, antibody clumps lodging in tissues, and slower T-cell reactions — and each leaves different clues in lab tests. Scientific terms: CD4, CD8, HLA class I/II, type I (immediate, IgE), type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic), type III (immune complex), type IV (cell-mediated; IVa–c), EAACI types V–VII, tryptase, CDC crossmatch, complement consumption, IGRA.
explanation.why: The effector decides the damage: IgE on mast cells releases mediators; antibody bound to a cell targets that cell; circulating complexes deposit and activate complement; sensitized T cells release cytokines. Tests measure the effector or its consequence.
explanation.measure: Type I: sIgE; tryptase ~1–2 h with baseline ≥ 24 h (Ansotegui 2020; Beck 2019). Type II: CDC crossmatch cell killing (Althaf 2017). Type III: low C3 in active SLE (Al-Shaikhly 2020). Type IV: IGRA IFN-γ (Pai 2014).
explanation.differs: Type II (antibody against a fixed cell antigen) vs type III (soluble immune complexes); antibody-mediated (I–III) vs cell-mediated (IV); CD8/class I vs CD4/class II.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a reaction from its mechanism, avoid the II vs III mix-up, recall the CD4/CD8 pairing, and choose the test that reflects each type.

questions.stem: Circulating antigen–antibody complexes deposit in glomeruli and consume complement. Which hypersensitivity type is this?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Type II antibody targets antigen on a cell surface.
Incorrect. Type I is IgE-mediated immediate.

questions.stem: Which T cells recognize peptides presented on HLA class I?

options.rationale: Correct. CD8 pairs with class I.
Incorrect. CD4 pairs with class II.
Incorrect. B cells recognize antigen through surface immunoglobulin.
Incorrect. Mast cells bind IgE via FcεRI.

questions.stem: Which laboratory test most directly reflects a type IV (cell-mediated) response?

options.rationale: Correct. It measures IFN-γ released by sensitized T cells.
Incorrect. Tryptase reflects mast-cell activation (type I).
Incorrect. Complement consumption fits immune-complex (type III) disease.
Incorrect. That detects cytotoxic antibody (type II mechanism).
